strengths: Presents a practical, modular, training-free cascaded retrieval pipeline (sparse -> dense -> neural reranking) for table QA that avoids costly dataset-specific fine-tuning, which is a useful contribution for adaptability to new domains.

Provides reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each retrieval stage, query decomposition, table descriptions, and irrelevant-row filtering (Tables 5-10), which helps interpret where gains come from.
Includes an interesting robustness experiment under query paraphrasing, showing that CRAFT's cascade degrades far less than fine-tuned DTR variants, which is a meaningful practical finding.
Provides end-to-end QA evaluation across multiple LLMs (Mistral, Llama3, Qwen2.5) and retrieval depths, plus a token-efficiency analysis (sub-table vs full-table) that is useful for practitioners.
Includes full prompts in the appendix, aiding partial reproducibility of the LLM-driven preprocessing steps.
weaknesses: The headline claim that CRAFT 'achieves better retrieval performance than SOTA sparse, dense, and hybrid retrievers' is not well supported by the paper's own Table 1: THYME outperforms CRAFT substantially at R@1 (48.55 vs 41.13) and is competitive/better on average, undermining the central claim rather than merely nuancing it.

There appears to be a citation inconsistency/error: THYME is attributed to two different author sets (Da Li et al., 2025 and Weizhe Zhao et al., 2024) but cited with the same arXiv ID (2503.02251), and the introduction/methodology refer to 'the state-of-the-art framework (Zhao et al., 2024)' interchangeably with THYME (Li et al., 2025). This raises concerns about citation rigor and correctness.

The paper motivates the approach by contrasting with the 'high computational cost' of dense/fine-tuned retrieval, yet no latency, memory, or inference-cost comparison against baselines (including cost of the Gemini/OpenAI API calls used in preprocessing and reranking) is provided, leaving the core efficiency claim unsubstantiated.

Reliance on closed, versioned commercial APIs (Gemini-1.5-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Flash, text-embedding-3-small) for core pipeline steps undermines reproducibility and the 'training-free' framing, since these models can change or become unavailable, and no open alternative or sensitivity analysis is given.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (NQ-Tables), and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this, but no discussion or partial experiment on a second dataset (e.g., other open-domain TQA benchmarks) is attempted to support generalizability claims made in the abstract/conclusion.

No statistical significance testing or variance/repetition is reported for LLM-based end-to-end generation results, which can be stochastic, weakening confidence in reported F1 differences (e.g., few-shot vs zero-shot comparisons in Table 12 that are often within a point or two of each other).

Some comparisons (e.g., end-to-end results in Table 3 combining other retrievers' outputs with CRAFT's answer-generation pipeline, and Table 4 comparing against very different baseline systems RAG/DPR-RAGE/LI-RAGE with unclear matched conditions) are not clearly controlled, making it hard to isolate whether gains stem from retrieval quality, table representation (mini-tables), or prompt engineering.
The claim of 'outperforms all existing TQA-in-the-wild' in the introduction is vague, uncited, and not clearly substantiated by a specific comparison in the results.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant problem (scalable, adaptable table retrieval without dataset-specific fine-tuning) and proposes a sensible, modular cascade combining sparse retrieval, dense reranking, and LLM-based augmentation.

Extensive stage-wise ablations (Tables 8-12) isolate the contribution of each pipeline component (table descriptions, query decomposition, mini-table row filtering, neural reranking), giving useful insight into where gains come from.
The robustness experiment under query paraphrasing (Section 4.2) is a nice addition that DTR-based baselines lack, and shows CRAFT's cascade recovers most of the performance lost to rephrasing.
Efficiency analysis (token counts, embedding call counts) is detailed and provides a concrete quantitative case for the mini-table design.
Qualitative case studies (Appendix D) illustrating full-table hallucination vs mini-table correctness add useful diagnostic value beyond aggregate metrics.
weaknesses: The 'training-free'/'zero-shot' framing is undercut by the fact that dataset-specific model choices are made per benchmark (e.g., different embedding backbones for NQ-Tables vs OTT-QA, choice between text-embedding-3-small/large reported post hoc), and it is unclear whether these choices were selected using a held-out dev set or directly optimized against test-set recall, raising concerns about test-set leakage/overfitting in what is claimed to be a zero-shot method.

Comparisons framed as CRAFT 'outperforming SOTA' are not fully apples-to-apples: baselines are fine-tuned on the target dataset while CRAFT is not, yet CRAFT still benefits from per-dataset architecture/model tuning; the paper does not adequately caveat that this is not a fair zero-shot vs. supervised comparison in the same sense as typical zero-shot transfer evaluations.

On OTT-QA, CRAFT trails the best supervised hybrid baseline (THYME) by a nontrivial margin at R@1 (55.56 vs 66.67), and the end-to-end OTT-QA results are only reported in an oracle setting with gold passages, which is not a realistic open-domain evaluation and limits the paper's claims of 'strong zero-shot performance' on this benchmark.

The large-scale offline cost of using Gemini-1.5-Flash to generate titles/descriptions and sub-questions for every table (169K-419K tables) and every query is not discussed as part of the computational budget, despite efficiency being a central claimed contribution; this makes the 'training-free' cost savings arguably overstated relative to the true end-to-end resource footprint.

Reproducibility is undermined by the placeholder 'Code and data are available at:' with no actual link provided in the manuscript, and heavy reliance on proprietary, versioned APIs (Gemini, OpenAI embeddings) that can change over time, threatening long-term reproducibility.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided despite many close margins between CRAFT and competing methods (e.g., R@10/R@50 gaps of ~1 point on OTT-QA), making some 'competitive' claims hard to substantiate rigorously.

The contribution is largely an engineering integration of existing off-the-shelf components (SPLADE, sentence-transformers, OpenAI/Gemini embeddings, LLM-based augmentation) rather than a novel modeling or algorithmic advance, limiting the technical novelty relative to prior cascaded/hybrid retrieval work already cited (Re2G, THYME, DHR).
